hydroponic-automation.title: Types of hydroponic system
hydroponic-automation.explanation: The six growing methods surveyed before choosing one — nutrient film, deep water culture, ebb and flow, drip, aeroponics and the conventional variant. Each places different demands on the controller.

hydroponic-automation.title: Dallas temperature sensor
hydroponic-automation.explanation: The waterproof 1-Wire probe used for water temperature. 1-Wire lets several probes share a single data line, which matters when sensors are spread across a tank, a feed line and the air above the crop.

hydroponic-automation.title: Turbidity sensor — voltage against cloudiness
hydroponic-automation.explanation: The sensor's transfer curve. Turbidity indicates algae growth or particulate contamination in the nutrient solution, both of which foul the pumps.

hydroponic-automation.title: Hydroponic growing pipe
hydroponic-automation.explanation: The growing channel itself, with the net-pot spacing that sets how many plants a run supports and how much root mass the flow has to feed.

hydroponic-automation.title: pH solutions, A&B nutrient and dosing pumps
hydroponic-automation.explanation: The correction chemistry: pH-up and pH-down solutions plus the two-part A&B nutrient concentrate, each on its own dosing pump. A and B must be dosed separately — mixed at concentration they precipitate out of solution.

hydroponic-automation.title: pH regulation algorithm
hydroponic-automation.explanation: The control loop for pH, implemented as a state machine. If the reading sits outside the configured window the matching pump runs for five seconds, then the loop waits thirty before reading again. That settle time is the whole design: dosing faster than the tank mixes is exactly how a pH controller ends up oscillating between over-corrections.

hydroponic-automation.title: A&B nutrient regulation algorithm
hydroponic-automation.explanation: Nutrient strength is controlled against electrical conductivity: EC rises as dissolved salts increase, so it stands in for concentration. A and B are dosed in a fixed ratio and the loop waits for the reading to settle.

hydroponic-automation.title: Tank water level regulation algorithm
hydroponic-automation.explanation: Level control, and the reason nutrient dosing is sequenced after it: topping up with plain water dilutes the solution, so EC has to be corrected after the level is right, never before.

hydroponic-automation.title: Simulation — view 1
hydroponic-automation.explanation: The system modelled before hardware was committed, to check that the control loops behave at realistic tank volumes and dosing rates.

hydroponic-automation.title: Simulation — view 2
hydroponic-automation.explanation: A second simulation view covering the interaction between level, EC and pH regulation running together.

hydroponic-automation.title: pH sensor calibration
hydroponic-automation.explanation: Calibration against buffer solutions. A pH probe drifts as its glass membrane ages, so periodic recalibration is a maintenance requirement, not a one-off setup step.

hydroponic-automation.title: Control panel — interior
hydroponic-automation.explanation: The assembled controller: supplies, relays and terminal blocks, with low-voltage signal wiring kept away from the switched mains side.

hydroponic-automation.title: Control panel — inner cover
hydroponic-automation.explanation: The inner cover, which keeps the mains section out of reach while the low-voltage side is being worked on.

hydroponic-automation.title: Light measurement hardware
hydroponic-automation.explanation: The light sensing head as built, positioned at canopy height where the measurement is actually meaningful.

hydroponic-automation.title: Water tank and measurement instruments
hydroponic-automation.explanation: The tank with the pH, EC and level instrumentation installed in the circulation path.
